Section (1) Neonatal Health System
1.1 Introduction
Neonatal health remains a critical global public health priority, as the period around birth carries
the highest risk of mortality for both mothers and newborns. Globally, nearly 1.3 million fresh
stillbirths and approximately 1 million neonatal deaths occur each year in close temporal
association with childbirth. The majority of these deaths are preventable through timely, high-
quality, and evidence-based interventions delivered during pregnancy, labour, childbirth, and the
early postnatal period, with particular attention to small and sick newborns.
In Sudan, the burden of neonatal mortality and stillbirths remains unacceptably high and
represents a major contributor to under-five mortality. In 2023, Sudan’s neonatal mortality rate
(NMR) was estimated at 24.8 per 1,000 live births, translating into approximately 41,690
neonatal deaths annually. In parallel, the stillbirth rate was estimated at 21.51 per 1,000 total
births, corresponding to nearly 36,973 stillbirths each year. These figures reflect not only the
magnitude of the problem but also the persistent gaps in access to quality maternal and newborn
health services, particularly in fragile, conflict-affected, and humanitarian settings.
Recognizing this burden, the Federal Ministry of Health has prioritized newborn survival as a
national agenda through the development and implementation of the Sudan Newborn Action
Plan (SuNAP) 2022–2030, aligned with global commitments under the Sustainable
Development Goals. SuNAP sets ambitious but achievable targets, aiming for 50% of Sudanese
states to achieve 12 or fewer neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births, and 60% of states to reach
12 or fewer stillbirths per 1,000 total births by 2030, with a strong emphasis on equity,
including populations affected by humanitarian crises.
Most neonatal deaths (75%) occur during the first week of life, and about 1 million newborns die
within the first 24 hours. Among neonates, the leading causes of death include premature birth,
birth complications (birth asphyxia/trauma), neonatal infections and congenital anomalies, which
collectively account for almost 4 in every 10 deaths in children under 5 years of age

2.1 Triage of newborn at special care newborn unit
● Triage is a quick assessment and sorting process used to evaluate and categorize sick
newborns shortly after they arrive at special care newborn units.
● It helps prioritize care and treatment based on the severity of their condition and the available
resources.
● The healthcare provider should carry out a brief, focused assessment and categorize the
newborn into one of the following three groups:
1. Emergency Signs (Danger Signs)
These are indicators that the newborn is critically ill and at immediate risk of death if urgent
intervention is not provided.
2. Priority Signs
These signs suggest that the baby requires prompt attention and should be moved ahead in the
queue for timely assessment and treatment.
3. Non-Urgent Signs
These are signs that do not fall under emergency or priority categories and can wait for further
evaluation without immediate risk.
The key signs indicating illness in newborns include:
● Poor feeding Decreased activity or altered consciousness
● Fast breathing (over 60 breaths per minute)
● Slow breathing (under 40 breaths per minute)
● Chest indrawing
● Grunting
● Seizures
● Bulging fontanelle
● Evidence of circulatory impairment (Capillary Refill time ,BP, pulse rate/volume)
● Floppiness or stiffness
● Fever (above 37.5°C)
● Hypothermia (below 36.5°C)
● Discharge, bleeding, or redness around the umbilical area
● More than 10 skin pustules or bullae, or any swelling, redness, or hardness of the skin
● Pallor
● Learning how to use thermometer ,check pallor ,
● A video showing fast breath, slow breath, chest indrawing, seizures , postules and bullae
Based on the presence or absence of these signs, newborns can be classified as normal, at risk, or
sick. This classification supports timely prioritization and ensures appropriate, evidence-based
care is provided promptly.
Newborns categorized as "Emergency" require immediate intervention and emergency care.
These babies should be promptly stabilized and then admitted to the Special Newborn Care Unit
(SNCU).
Those classified as "Priority" are ill and need a swift assessment followed by admission to the
SNCU for appropriate care.
Newborns identified as "Non-Urgent" do not need immediate medical attention but still require
a thorough evaluation and parental counseling.
2.2 Further Assessment and Management:
Once emergency care has been provided and the newborn is stabilized, a detailed assessment
should be carried out. This includes obtaining a comprehensive history and identifying any at-
risk neonates based on maternal characteristics and other relevant factors.

Introduction
The admission process for a newborn to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (SPECIAL CARE
NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU)) can be challenging and involves several key steps to ensure the
baby's immediate stabilization and comprehensive care.
These steps need to be well organized, smooth and time effective aiming to increase Golden
Hour success rates, decrease staff stress levels, and ultimately improve patient outcomes.
Importance
Admission of newborns, particularly sick newborns, is a crucial part of the Golden Hour of the
baby life.
3.1 Admission process: welcoming
The steps of admitting a newborn to Special Care Newborn Unit (SCNU) can be looked at in the
following order
1. Preparation before receiving the baby
2. Receiving the baby
Endorsement or handover
Assessment
Maintaining stability and
Monitoring
3. Writing and reviewing admission orders
Sampling
Procedures
Medications
4. Parental support
3.2 Preparation before receiving the baby
Immediately upon receiving a call or notification of an expected admission, an admission team is
organized. The SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) team is multidisciplinary,
including neonatologists/pediatrician, nurses, respiratory therapists ( if available), and other
specialists, to provide comprehensive care.
The SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) team prepares for the baby's arrival, including
setting up necessary equipment and ensuring a warm environment.
Equipment to be checked would include:
a) Admission incubator/ warmer: (extreme preterm usually require special incubator), check
if the incubator/ warmer is functioning, prewarm it, adjust temperature and humidity,
b) Admission trolley or cart: with all necessary supplies which are neatly organized and
visible. Each compartment is labeled with the item name and quantity to make restocking
easier. (like syringes, iv sets, iv fluids, gauzes, sample collection containers and other
medications).
c) Vital signs monitor and its wires and connections.
d) Ventilatory support as recommended by the labour and delivery team. Nasal cannula,
HHFNC, CPAP or Ventilator. Should be checked, ready and stand by.
e) Admission file with necessary charts like Ballard and growth parameters charts.
3.3 Receiving the newborn baby
Once the baby arrived at SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) the next interventions
had to be done simultaneously.
a) Endorsement or handover:
- A thorough handover from the transferring unit to the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN
UNIT (SCNU) team is crucial, including details about the baby's condition,
medications, and any special needs.
- Each staff (medical and nursing staff) should receive their own endorsement.
- Maternal, antenatal and perinatal history is reviewed and documented.
- Admission orders should be reviewed carefully by the admission team
b) Assessment
- Assessment, monitoring and maintenance of stability are ongoing processes during all
steps of the golden hour of life.
- A rapid assessment, including evaluation of vital signs (heart rate, breathing,
admission temperature), a physical examination, and potentially some initial lab tests
like blood gas analysis.
- Growth parameters are measured immediately; however, the measurement may be
delayed till the baby is stable enough.
- A check list for endorsement and assessment would help organize the admission
process and prevent confusion or missing important actions.
c) Maintaining stability and monitoring Once in the SCNU, the baby is closely monitored:
- including vital signs, oxygen saturation, body temperature and other physiological
parameters.
- Maintenance of warmth to prevent serious hypothermia is crucial.
- Incubator temperature (servo or manual) and humidity adjustment is very vital on
admission.
- Wrapping baby with plastic bags may needed especially extreme and VLBW infant
- Degree of respiratory distress and efficacy of respiratory support should be monitored
and adjusted as needed.
- Blood glucose monitoring and judicious management of hypoglycemia is crucial to
Prevent serious CNS complications of hypoglycemia.
3.4 Writing and reviewing admission orders
The most senior pediatrician/ neonatologist may need to give some verbal orders during
assessment, however, the final admission orders should be written and recorded immediately
after finishing the assessment. The orders should be very clear and in a systematic manner.
a) Decide level of care
b) Systems:
• CNS: sedation, imaging
• CVS: monitoring, imaging, inotropes
• Respiratory: type of support and settings of the machine, frequency of blood gases, imaging.
• GIT: NPO vs feeding, imaging, NGT
• Renal and fluid: TFI, type of IVF, UOP monitoring
• Infectious diseases: cultures and antibiotics
• Procedures: lines (UVC. UAC), LP, needle aspiration
• Medications: antibiotics, others
The orders must be recorded and reviewed by nursing staff (at least 2 nurses) and any confusion
or unclear order should be clarified with the medical staff immediately.
All requested blood samples should be withdrawn as soon as possible.
IV medications are administered as soon as the IV line is ready.
The nursing staff prepares for all procedures and assists the medical staff during procedures such
as fixation of central lines.
3.5 Parental Support
The SCNU team provides ongoing support and education to parents, helping parents to
understand their baby's condition and participate in their care
• The team updates the parents regarding the situation on admission and after stabilization,
describe the acuity of the current condition and outline the management plan and
expectations.
• Parents should be supported and given the facts in a gentle way that consider their nature
and respect their rights, beliefs and feelings. They should feel welcomed and be
encouraged to visit their baby frequently.
• A special team to support mothers for breast milk expression and breast feeding should
always be available and ready to assist.
• Parents will be asked to provide consent for any necessary procedures or treatments,
including potential formula feeding if breastfeeding is not immediately feasible.

Section (4) The Golden Hour of Life:
Goals
1. To understand the concept of Golden Hour
2. To know the significance of Golden hour interventions
3. To gain an approach that uses the best available evidence aiming to implement safe,
effective and timely interventions
4. Prevention of Hypothermia
5. Support of Respiration
6. Support of Cardiovascular System
7. Support of Nutrition and hydration
8. Prevention of Sepsis
Golden Hour Definition
Golden Hour of neonatal life is defined as the first hour of post-natal life in both preterm and
term neonates.
The Golden hour concept includes practicing all the evidence based intervention for term and
preterm neonates, in the initial sixty minutes of postnatal life for better long-term outcome.
Although the current evidence supports the concept of golden hour in preterm, still there is no
evidence seeking the benefit of golden hour approach in term neonates,
Initial first hour of neonatal life includes
1. Early Essential newborn Care and neonatal resuscitation,
2. post-resuscitation care,
3. transportation of sick newborn to neonatal intensive care unit,
4. respiratory and cardiovascular support and nutrition support
5. initial course in SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU).
Importance of applying the Golden Hour concept and interventions
The neonatal management in the first hour of life have an important effect on both immediate
and long-term outcomes of all neonates.
The studies that evaluated the concept of golden hour in preterm neonates showed
marked reduction in
1. hypothermia,
2. hypoglycemia,
3. intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH),
4. bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), and
5. retinopathy of prematurity (ROP).
4.1 Prevention of hypothermia in special newborn care unit
(beyond resuscitation)
The newborn body temperature should be kept within the neutral thermal zone during
transport and on admission to SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) by maintaining
between 36.7 and 37.2-degree C.
Any baby requiring humidity or with respiratory compromise or clinical instability should
not be dressed or covered by fabrics.
All babies, irrespective of gestation, should have continuous skin temperature monitoring
from admission until they are swaddled.
During resuscitations in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, it is essential to consider the
maintenance of the newborn’s temperature. Cold stress may be eliminated by employing
overhead heat on the resuscitative or ensuring appropriate heating in the incubator.
Interventions in the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) that have been found to
reduce hypothermia in very preterm infants include:
• use of servo-controlled incubators by targeting abdominal skin temperature set at 36.5° C
• use of higher humidity compared to lower humidity in incubators.
• use of topical emollients including coconut oil.
• use of plastic wrap or plastic drapes for procedures in the special care newborn unit
(SCNU).
• use of kangaroo mother care for stable low birthweight infants.
Three main types of beds are used in the special care newborn unit (SCNU) is:
1. Incubators
2. Open Care /Radiant Warmer
3. Standard Cot
Incubators:
Are fully enclosed cots that allow heated air and humidity to be added to the baby’s environment
whilst reducing stimuli including light and sound.
These incubators are double walled to reduce radiant and conductive heat loss.
Current incubators are efficient when only one side is opened for cares or procedures, but not
when both sides are opened together which results in high convective and evaporative
heat loss.
● All preterm infants ≤ 30 weeks’ gestation and / or ≤ 1000 g should be nursed in
incubators.
● Incubators are the admission bed of choice for all babies born < 33 weeks gestation or ≤
● Some preterm babies born ≥ 33 weeks’ gestation may require an incubator if hypothermic
on admission.
● Term and near-term infants may be swaddled and nursed in a cot if stable.
● For those requiring respiratory care an open care system should be used.
● Infants with suspected perinatal asphyxia should not be place in an incubator as this
places them at risk of hyperthermia.
● When using an incubator, avoid or minimize the time doors on opposite sides of the
incubators are open during procedures and cares – this practice will increase heat loss via
convention.
Open care/ Radiant warmers
1. Radiant Warmer, is a body warming device to provide heat to the body. They help to
maintain the body temperature of the baby and limit the metabolism rate.
2. The skin temperature of the baby can be monitored by a temperature measuring knob that
is kept continuously attached to the body.
3. Radiant Warmers can be manual or automatic (servo system – heater output is
determined automatically based on skin temperature. The skin temperature is set at 36.5
degree Celsius) depending on the mechanism that the manufacturer employs for
temperature control.
4. The automatic model increases the heat output in small predetermined steps to reach at
the desired temperature of the body.
5. The device may seem simple to handle, but it is always recommended to have a proper
training and read the manufacturers guidelines for person handling this equipments.
6. It is necessary to regularly clean and disinfect the instrument.
7. Generally, rdiant warmers result in increased IWL compared to incubators. This needs to
be taken into account when calculating daily fluid requirements. ( A heat shield of thin
polyethylene film can be used with a radiant warmer to reduce heat loss by convection
and evaporation.
8. The major advantage of the radiant warmer is the easy access it provides to critically-ill
infants without disturbing the thermal environment. Its major disadvantage is the increase
in insensible water loss produced by the radiant warmer. Most infants can be safely and
adequately cared for in either incubator or radiant warmer bed.
Standard cot
Standard cots are opened beds used for:
1. Routine care for term and late preterm newborns in post- natal word and nursery
2. Weaning preterm and sick babies from incubators or warmers

t: Infant care post crib transfer
• Check temperature every hour x 4 after crib transfer. If temperature is between 36.2°C
and 36.5°C, increase clothing layers if possible and add a pre-warmed blanket.
• Continue to check temperature hourly until axillary temperature is ≥ 36.5°C for 4
consecutive hours.
• If temperature is < 36.5°C for 3 consecutive hours (3 x hourly checks), return infant to a
pre-warmed incubator.
Additional instructions
• BATHING should be deferred until temperature is maintained ≥ 36.5°C for a minimum
of 12 hours after transition to crib.
• Thereafter, normal unit bathing guidelines should be followed (e.g. CLABSI prevention
strategies).
• If infant has a central line (PICC), ensure site remains visible.
• Infants with poor growth after transition may require return to an incubator due to
increased energy expenditure maintaining thermal control.
4.2 Support of respiration after special care newborn unit (SCNU)
admission:
Respiratory diseases are the leading cause of early neonatal morbidity and mortality, as well as
the most frequent indication for both term and preterm neonates’ admission to the special care
newborn unit (SCNU).
The most common causes of admission to special care newborn unit (SCNU) are:
• Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) and prematurity.
• Transient Tachypnea of newborn (TTN)
• Congenital pneumonia
• Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS)
• Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH)
• Tracheoesophageal Fistula
• Congenital Heart Diseases
• Metabolic disease.
The most common causes of admission in advanced SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT
(SCNU) are RDS (preterm and extreme preterm babies) and TTN (late preterm and Term).
According to currently available data, respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) affects about 80% of
neonates born at 28 weeks GA, and this percentage increases to 90% at 24 weeks GA. About 50–
60% of these neonates need surfactant administration.
Modalities of respiratory support used in special care newborn unit (SCNU) and NICU:
(see ventilation section)
1. Non-invasive Ventilation: (NIV)
a) nCPAP
b) Heated Humidified High Flow Nasal Cannula (HHHFNC)
c) Bi-PAP
d) NIVPP
e) Non-invasive neurally adjusted ventilator assist (NIV-NAVA)
f) Nasal high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (NHFOV)
2. Invasive Ventilation (Mechanical Ventilation MV)
a) Conventional MV
b) High Frequency Ventilation (HHO and HFJ)
The type of respiratory support should be decided and SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT
(SCNU) team informed before shifting the baby to SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT
(SCNU). (see Admission to SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) section)
What type of respiratory support?
1. Respiratory support of the critically ill neonate has steadily shifted from invasive to
noninvasive forms of support.
2. Mechanical ventilation (MV), although life-saving, is associated with chronic respiratory
morbidity in both preterm and term born infants including bronchopulmonary Dysplasia
BPD.
3. New ventilation modes have been developed with the aim of minimizing lung injury.
These include invasive and non-invasive respiratory support strategies and techniques for
less invasive surfactant administration (LISA).
Non- invasive Ventilation (see Non-invasive Ventilation section)
Nasal Continuous Positive Pressure nCPAP: can be applied as:
A) Early CPAP: i.e. as a primary mode of ventilation started in the delivery room: now
recommended as the optimal mode of respiratory support in infants at risk of respiratory
distress syndrome (RDS) who do not require intubation for stabilization).
Systemic review showed that: Prophylactic or very early CPAP when compared to
mechanical ventilation Reduced:
▪ the incidence of BPD,
▪ the combined outcome of death or BPD, and
▪ mechanical ventilation.
B) Post Extubation CPAP (see Non-invasive Ventilation section).
Nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) (see Non-invasive Ventilation
section)
1. NIPPV provides two levels of pressure:
▪ a PEEP and
▪ a PIP
2. It is provided by a ventilator through a non-invasive interface (mask or prongs)
3. can be synchronized with the infant's breathing.
NIPPV vs CPAP:
Early nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) in preterm infants at risk of
respiratory distress within the first hours after birth reduced the
1. risk of respiratory failure,
2. the need for intubation,
3. rates of treatment failure and
4. mechanical ventilation
compared with early CPAP without increasing the risk of complications. (Cochrane review).
Heated Humidified High Flow Nasal Cannula (HHHNC):
1. Flows of between 2 and 8 liters/ minute via nasal catheters
2. Can be used as alternative of CPAP.
3. Advantages: compared to CPAP:
▪ perceived better access to the infant,
▪ less nasal trauma and air leaks
▪ quicker achievement of oral feeds
4. Disadvantages
▪ The pressure delivered to the lungs is unknown
▪ Possible higher rate of treatment failure when used as primary mode.
Surfactant Administration:
1. Surfactant administered in the delivery suite might prevent or reduce the severity of
subsequent respiratory distress syndrome.
2. From the available evidence the most effective way to optimize surfactant delivery and
obtain a more homogeneous distribution of the drug is by using rapid bolus instillation in
combination with appropriate alveolar recruitment techniques.
3. The methods of surfactant administration (as well as ventilation strategies) are moving
steadily from invasive (using ETT) to less invasive (no EETT) techniques.
4. We will try to answer these questions
1. Early vs Late surfactant?
2. How to avoid intubation and mechanical ventilation aiming to reduce the rate of BPD
without depriving some infants of the proven benefits of expedient provision of
exogenous surfactant?
Methods of surfactant administration include
1. Using ETT
▪ Prophylactic surfactant.
▪ Early Rescue surfactant
▪ INSURE technique
2. Using a Special Catheter
▪ Less Invasive Surfactant Administration (LISA) or Minimally Invasive Surfactant
Therapy (MIST)
3. Using Laryngeal Mask
▪ Supraglottic airway (less invasive)
4. Nebulized Surfactant
Non-invasive
Prophylactic Surfactant:
Prophylactic use of surfactant refers to a strategy of providing exogenous surfactant at birth to
infants at risk for RDS, with the aim of preventing severe RDS from developing.
However, this strategy is NO longer indicated:
Literature reviews showed:
1. With use of prophylactic surfactant there was trend toward increasing mortality,
bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) at 28 days and 36 weeks, and BPD or death at 36 weeks
with the use of prophylactic surfactant. (level 1a evidence)
2. Use of early CPAP or early non-invasive ventilation in the labour room was associated with:
a) tendency towards less BPD and mortality in preterm newborn.
b) Significant decrease in rate of intubation.
c) Significant decrease in need for surfactant administration.
However, infants with RDS who are already intubated during resuscitation should receive
exogenous surfactant before inter-facility transport.
Selective or Rescue surfactant
Selective or rescue use of surfactant refers to a strategy of providing exogenous surfactant to
infants with established RDS. It can be given early (less than 2 hours of age) or late (2 hours or
beyond)
Early versus delayed rescue surfactant
1.Early Rescue surfactant:
administration of exogenous surfactant for preterm infants intubated for RDS within the first 2 h
of age.
2. Late Rescue surfactant:
administration of exogenous surfactant for preterm infants intubated for RDS delayed until RDS
was established, usually 2 h or beyond.
Meta-analyses of six randomized trials showed that early surfactant was associated with a
significant decrease in
▪ mortality, BPD at 36 weeks,
▪ BPD or death at 36 weeks, and
▪ reduction in the risk of air leak,
▪ with no increase in the risk for pulmonary hemorrhage or severe IVH.
What is the oxygen threshold for a baby on early CPAP to administer early rescue
surfactant?
A number of studies suggest that low (FiO2 0.30 to 0.50) versus high (FiO2 >0.55) thresholds
show more benefit by providing surfactant earlier—before the development of more severe
RDS—without increasing the rate of intubation significantly.
In one systematic review published in 2007, analysis based on oxygen requirement criteria
showed that a lower threshold (FiO2 ≤0.45) for intubation and surfactant administration was
associated with less air leak and BPD compared with an FiO2 threshold >0.45.
Two large randomized trials that did not allow infants initially managed with CPAP to receive
surfactant until an FiO2 threshold of 0.6 was reached demonstrated higher rates of pneumothorax
compared with those who were intubated and given surfactant early [24][32] (Level 1a
evidence).
Use of surfactant before inter-facility transport of preterm infants was found to be associated
with lower oxygen requirement during transport and shorter duration of ventilation support,
compared with controls [33] (Level 4 evidence).
What type of surfactant (synthetic vs animal derived:
In summary animal-derived and the newer generation synthetic surfactants are both effective for
treating RDS and improving survival without BPD. When comparing different animal-derived
surfactants, emerging evidence suggests that porcine minced lung extract, especially in higher
dose, may be superior to bovine surfactant for improving acute respiratory status and reducing
mortality or BPD in infants with RDS (Level 1a evidence)

B. Any preterm infant on CPAP immediately after delivery

Correct answer: C

4.3 Support of the CVS after admission to special care newborn
unit (SCNU)
The neonatologist should identify shock in compensated phase and should manage it
aggressively.
1. The management includes
a) establishing early intravenous access,
b) judicious use of fluid resuscitation,
c) vasopressors (dopamine or ( or noradrenaline)) and
d) other supportive care like blood transfusion for hemorrhage, and antibiotics for septic
shock
Monitoring support of CVS during the Golden hour after admission to SPECIAL CARE
NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU)
1. Clinical observation:
a) Heart rate
b) Pulse volume
c) Capillary refill
d) Markers of end-organ perfusion
2. Non-invasive monitoring
a) Non-invasive arterial blood pressure measurement
b) Electrocardiogram
c) Echocardiogram
d) Pulse oximetry
e) Cerebral monitoring.
3. Invasive monitoring
a) Intra- arterial BP monitoring
b) Arterial blood gas monitoring ( ABG)
c) Central venous pressure.
Clinical observations:
This is the sim plest and most easily performed method
a) Heart Rate:
1. This is easily assessed at the bedside and requires no specialist equipment.
2. An increased heart rate may reflect increased demand, for example hypovolemic
states, seizures and the Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS).
3. In the special care newborn unit (SCNU) setting however, other factors may result in
tachycardia, such as agitation, pain and non-sinus arrhythmias.
b) Pulse Volume
1. This is difficult to quantify on a clinical basis, but nevertheless is a useful method of
assessment.
2. A disparity between central pulses (palpable) and peripheral pulses (impalpable)
usually indicates a cardiac problem or hypovolemia.
c) Capillary Refill Time (CRT)
1. CRT has long been regarded as a quick and reproducible method of assessing
circulatory status5.
2. However, the traditional emphasis has been in the context of resuscitation rather than
the post-resuscitation (ICU) phase, where doubts exist regarding its usefulness in
reflecting CVS function.
Markers of End- organ Perfusion:
1. Skin color and temperature can be assessed quickly and may reflect the adequacy of
the organ’s blood supply and therefore (indirectly) the patient’s cardiac output.
2. However, their reliability in assessing cardiac function is low, especially in the ICU
patient.

t: Non-invasive Monitoring
a) Non-invasive blood pressure measurement NIBP:
1. NIBP is widely used in all areas of health care.
2. Measurement of systemic blood pressure (BP) is virtually universal and is vital in the
assessment of organ perfusion.
3. It is also an indicator of CO and systemic vascular resistance and therefore an
important guide to therapy.
4. The traditional method of using a mercury sphygmomanometer and stethoscope has
been superceded by automated devices such as the Dinamap.
5. In the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) setting, NIBP can be integrated
into the overall monitoring system, allowing repeated estimations of NIBP at set
intervals, the pressure is then displayed on the monitor screen alongside other
parameters.
b) Electrocardiogram ECG:
1. Continuous ECG monitoring is now ubiquitous in SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN
UNIT (SCNU) and neonatal intensive care settings. It may be centralized (i.e. all
patients’ ECGs displayed at a central monitor) or monitored at the bedside, or both.
2. The ECG is primarily useful as an indication of heart rate, when peripheral perfusion
is poor, for monitoring of bradycardia associated with apnoea and desaturations, and
as an alert to the possibility of an arrhythmia. 3. Should an arrhythmia be suspected
then a 12-lead ECG is mandatory.
c) Echocardiography
1. The echocardiogram is a vital tool in assessment of cardiac function in the SPECIAL
CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU)
2. It will provide information regarding cardiac size, preload, contractility and afterload
which, together with heart rate, are the major factors that influence cardiac output.
3. Its role has also been expanded to the neonatologist for rapid diagnosis of, for
example, cardiac tamponade.
d) Pulse Oximetry:
1. Pulse oximetry is a widely-used non-invasive technique but there are caveats to its use,
for instance in a poorly- perfused extremity, anaemia or increased skin pigmentation.
2. It cannot distinguish between carboxy- and oxyhaemoglobin and in
methaemoglobinaemia the measurement is unreliable.
3. The latest pulse oximeters aim to minimize the artifact that derives from patient
movement.
e) Cerebral Monitoring:
1. In neonates, alterations in the integrated electroencephalogram, monitored by a
cerebral function monitor, may give the first indication of cardiovascular inadequacy.
2. Near-infra-red spectroscopy (NIRS) is a global, non-invasive, continuous method of
monitoring cerebral oxygen saturation.
3. In practice a probe is applied to the skin (usually the forehead) which emits light,
similar to a pulse oximetry probe.
4. Its accuracy is heavily dependent on it distinguishing a signal from the brain rather
than the intervening tissue (e.g. skin, muscle and bone)
5. The tissue saturation derived is thought to be weighted to the greater proportion of
venous blood in the area sampled.
6. The readout is expressed as a percentage and the usual value is in the 60-80% range.
Values lower than 42% are thought to indicate dangerous tissue hypoxia.
Near infra-red spectroscopy – The INVOS System uses two depths of light penetration to
subtract out surface data, resulting in a regional oxygenation value for deeper tissues.
Invasive cardiovascular monitoring
a) Intra-arterial blood pressure (IABP)
1. is a well-established method of monitoring a patient’s cardiovascular status.
2. A pressure transducer measures the IABP and displays an arterial waveform via an
intra-arterial cannula (commonly inserted in the radial, umbilical or posterior tibial
artery).
3. The cannula also allows regular sampling of intra-arterial blood for analysis.
4. The arterial waveform may also be analyzed (pulse contour analysis) as it reflects the
stroke volume and cardiac output, but must still be calibrated against CO measured by
another method1
b) Arterial blood gas analysis:
1. Analysis of blood obtained from an arterial source provides vital information
regarding a patient’s cardiovascular status.
2. Lactate ( part of ABG ) is produced at a cellular level as a result of anaerobic
metabolism.
3. Lactate is an important marker of cardiovascular function as an increase in blood
lactate reflects tissue hypoxia.
4. This may be as a result of low cardiac output or reduced tissue oxygen extraction1.
c) Central venous pressure
1. Monitoring of CVP is more common in paediatric intensive care units and is rarely
utilized in neonatal practice..
Summary of cardiovascular monitoring methods.
ECG: Electrocardiogram;
NIBP: Non-invasive blood pressure; IABP: Intra-arterial blood pressure; CRT: Capillary refill
time; NIRS: Near-infra red spectroscopy; CVP: Central venous pressure.
4.4 Support Nutrition:
Although, during the golden hour, the first priority and concerns are the ventilation,
cardiorespiratory stability and prevention of hypothermia, a clear plan for support of nutrition
should be the first priority after stabilization of the baby. The strategy and plan for nutritional
support will depend on acuity of the babyś condition, the gestational age and whether there a
special condition:
1. Stable term or preterm
2. Preterm or sick newborn.
Overall, nutritional support in the delivery room and after SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT
(SCNU) admission should be individualized and closely monitored to ensure adequate
nourishment and metabolic stability for each newborn.
Nutritional Requirements:
Nutrient requirements include the following:
• Energy (measured as cal/kg/day)
• Carbohydrates
• Water
• Minerals and trace elements
• Protein
• Vitamins
• Fat
Support of nutrition of a stable term baby
The stable term or preterm who don’t have any contraindication of enteral feedings should be
started on enteral feeds within golden hour with preference to mother milk or donor human milk
Nutritional support in the delivery room should include prompt initiation of breastfeeding or
provision of appropriate infant formula to ensure adequate nourishment for the newborn.
Nutritional support for a stable newborn should prioritize prompt initiation of breastfeeding
within half an hour of birth for stable term babies, following NRP and Baby Friendly Hospital
Initiative (BFHI) guidelines.
Breast feeding helps to reduce the risk of baby becoming ill in the first weeks and months of life.
Stable premature infants in the special care newborn unit (SCNU) are usually fed by OG or NG
tube until they are sufficiently mature to coordinate sucking, swallowing, and breathing. Current
evidence indicates that trophic or minimal enteral feedings are safe and well tolerated. In this
technique, small volumes are fed to infants for a few days without significant increments.
Ten steps to successful breastfeeding
Critical management procedures
1. 1a. Comply fully with the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes and
relevant World Health Assembly resolutions.
1b. Have a written infant feeding policy that is routinely communicated to staff and
parents.
1c. Establish ongoing monitoring and data-management systems.
2. Ensure that staff have sufficient knowledge, competence and skills to support
breastfeeding.
Key clinical practices
3. Discuss the importance and management of breastfeeding with pregnant women and their
families.
4. Facilitate immediate and uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact and support mothers to
initiate breastfeeding as soon as possible after birth.
5. Support mothers to initiate and maintain breastfeeding and manage common difficulties.
6. Do not provide breastfed newborns any food or fluids other than breast milk, unless
medically indicated.
7. Enable mothers and their infants to remain together and to practice rooming-in 24 hours a
day.
8. Support mothers to recognize and respond to their infants’ cues for feeding.
9. Counsel mothers on the use and risks of feeding bottles, teats and pacifiers.
10. Coordinate discharge so that parents and their infants have timely access to ongoing
support and care.
Support of nutrition of Preterm and sick newborn
For preterm or unstable newborns, nutritional requirements should be carefully managed, taking
into account gestational age and fluid needs.
Feeding babies in the special care newborn unit (SCNU) is quite different from feeding healthy
babies. When babies are sick or premature, 1. they are often not well enough to breastfeed or
take a bottle.
2. Premature babies may not be able to suck effectively. Or
3. their GI (gastrointestinal) tracts may not be mature enough to digest feedings.
4. Babies who have unstable health are often unable to take regular feedings.
5. Babies with umbilical catheters and those who need help breathing, such as with a mechanical
ventilator, may not be able to be fed. (This is because of the risk of problems such as aspiration
(breathing food into the lungs).
For most of admitted newborns are ELBW, VLBW, EGLAN or sick term neonates, immediate
feeding cannot be started and they are usually kept NPO on admission.
A central venous access particularly umbilical venous catheter ( UVC ) should be secured in
these newborn and intravenous fluids (IVF ) should be started at earliest to prevent
hypoglycemia
Ideally for such babies total parenteral nutrition ( TPN ) should be initiated in the first hour of
admission
Fluid requirement
The fluid requirement of the newborn will depend upon the 1) gestational age, and 2)
sensible/insensible water loss.
The goal of fluid replacement is to provide adequate
calories,
protein,
lipids; and
compensate for the ongoing fluid losses.
In newborn infants the starting fluid on day 1 for birth weight:
• < 1000 gram is 100-150 ml/kg/day,
• 1000-1500 gram is 80-100 ml/kg/day
• for > 1500 gram is 60-80 ml/kg/day.
The total fluid intake per day should be monitored according to
1. Daily weight
2. Fluid balance
3. Urine output (UOP)
4. Serum sodium level (most sensitive): (Clinically: signs of dehydration are poor
predictors; capillary fill time is useful.
5. Hemodynamically significant PDA, proven NEC or CHD.
Serum sodium and fluid requirement:
1. Hyponatremia with weight loss suggests sodium depletion and needs sodium
replacement.
2. Hyponatremia with weight gain suggests dilutional hyponatremia and requires fluid
restriction.
3. Hypernatremia with weight loss suggests dehydration and management includes fluid
correction over 48 hours.
4. Hypernatremia with weight gain suggests salt and water load and needs fluid and sodium
restriction
Fluid restriction
The results from various studies have shown that restricted water intake has a beneficial effect on
the incidence of PDA, BPD, NEC and death.
Glucose requirement and Risk of hypoglycemia
After admission to the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU), nutritional support should
be tailored to the specific needs of the infant, including monitoring blood sugar levels and
providing appropriate glucose and fluid intake to maintain stable metabolic function.
For newborns at high risk for developing hypoglycemia, such as
1) premature,
2) intrauterine growth restricted, or 3) sick infants,
glucose levels should be monitored in the golden hour after birth.
The goal is to keep glucose level 50 -110 mg/dl and hypoglycemia should be managed with
feeding, or dextrose infusion.
Glucose infusion rate (GIR) is calculated and infusion is started at GIR of 4-6 mg/kg/min in
preterm and 6-8 mg/kg/min in term neonates and increased gradually to 12 mg/kg/ min) as per
the clinic condition of the newborn and symptoms of hypoglycemia.
This calculation of GIR is a simple (unites mg/kg/min):
GIR = IV Rate (mL/hr) X Dextrose Conc (g/dL) X 1000 (mg/g)
Weight (kg) X 60 (min/hr) X 100 (mL/dL)
where the dextrose concentration is expressed as a whole number, e.g. 5 or 10.
Hyperglycemia should also be monitored and managed appropriately, with blood sugar levels
checked regularly and insulin therapy initiated if necessary.
Each neonatal unite should have clear guidelines for management of hypoglycemia and
hyperglycemia
Additionally, careful attention should be paid to metabolic disorders such as galactosemia or
disorders of fatty acid oxidation.
Energy needs
The exact energy needs of a given neonate depend on several factors, including
• gestational age,
• postnatal age,
• weight,
• route of energy intake,
• growth rate,
• activity, and
• thermal environment.
Infants who are ill or experiencing stressful situations (sepsis, surgery, BPD) have higher energy
requirements.
Infants who receive parenteral nutrition (TPN) need less energy for adequate growth because
they do not need to absorb the provided nutrients and have no fecal losses.
As a result, 70-90cal/kg/day with 3-3.5g/kg/day of protein may be adequate for growth.
Protein is not an ideal source of energy; rather, it is provided as a building block for new tissue.
If adequate non-protein calories are provided, the nitrogen balance in the infant is positive and
the protein provided is used to build new tissue.
Therefore, even if energy intake from protein is included in calculations of total energy intake,
not all of the protein-derived calories are available for energy expenditure.
The ideal energy ratio provides
• 65% of the energy as carbohydrates and
• 35% as lipids.
Most infants need 100-120cal/kg/day for adequate growth.
Some need up to 160-180cal/kg/day (eg, infants with BPD).
The total energy needs of a growing, enterally fed premature infant without any acute illness are
listed as follows:
Resting expenditure - 50cal/kg/day
Minimal activity - 4-5cal/kg/day
Occasional cold stress - 10cal/kg/day
Fecal loss (10-15% of intake) - 15cal/kg/day
Growth (4.5 cal/g of growth) - 45cal/kg/day
Total required to produce a 10g/day weight gain - 125cal/kg/day
Mature human milk is made up of
• 6.9%-7.2% carbohydrate calculated as lactose, and
• 0.2% mineral constituents expressed as ash.
The energy content is 60-75 kcal/100ml. Protein content is considerably higher and carbohydrate
content lower in colostrum than in mature milk
Total Parenteral Nutrition
Nutrient requirements include the:
• Energy (measured as cal/kg/day)
• Carbohydrates
• Water
• Minerals and trace elements
• Protein
• Vitamins
• Fat
Total parenteral nutrition (TPN ) should provide adequate nutritional requirements mentioned
above.
The American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition (ASPEN) recommends parenteral
nutrition (PN) be started within 24 to 48 hours of life for premature and VLBW neonates to
promote growth and development while avoiding malnutrition and metabolic derangement.
If patient-specific PN is not available immediately after birth, starter PN formulations may be
used.
The daily protein and lipid requirement in ELBW/VLBW neonates is around 4-4.5 gm/kg/day
and 3 gm/kg/day respectively..
The content of a starter TPN usually include:
• dextrose,
• lipids and
• protein
• NO electrolytes in starter TPN

5.1 Introduction to prematurity epidemiology
Definitions
Preterm babies are defined as babies born alive before 37 weeks of pregnancy are completed.
Classification: There are sub-categories of preterm birth, based on gestational age:
● Extremely preterm: < 28 weeks.
● Very preterm: 28 to 31 6/7 weeks.
● Moderate to late preterm: 32 to < 36 6/7 weeks
Some references further classify extreme preterm babies born between 23 to 25 weeks as micro
preemie. (however, birth wt should be less than 500grams).
Another classification for preterm newborn is based on birth weight
● Low birth weight: less than (LBW) 2500 grans (between 1500 and 2500 grams.
● Very LBW: 1000 to 1500 grams.
● Extreme low birth weight: less than 1000 gram ( 500 to 1000 grams )
● Micro preemie: less than 500 grams
Peri-viability (or limit of viability)
• Earliest stage of fetal maturity where there is a reasonable chance, although perhaps not a
high likelihood, of extrauterine survival. This period is generally between 22 and <26
weeks gestational age (GA).
• Most infants born at ≥26 weeks GA have a high likelihood of survival, whereas virtually
none born at <22 weeks GA survive.
• Clearly the “limit of viability” is a moving target: Shaeffer and Avery’s textbook,
Diseases of the Newborn (1971), estimated the limit of viability to be around 28 weeks’
gestation and/or 1000 g.
Epidemiology
● Preterm birth complications are the leading cause of death among children under 5 years
of age. Three-quarters of these deaths could be prevented with current, cost-effective
interventions.
● Across countries, the rate of preterm birth ranges from 4–16% of babies.
● Approximately 900 000 children die in 2019 of complications of preterm birth.
● Many survivors face a lifetime of disability, including learning disabilities and visual and
hearing problems.
● Inequalities in survival rates around the world are sharply clear.
● In low-income settings, half of the babies born at or below 32 weeks (2 months early) die
due to a lack of feasible, cost-effective care such as warmth, breastfeeding support and
basic care for infections and breathing difficulties.
● In high-income countries, almost all these babies survive.
● Suboptimal use of technology in middle-income settings is causing an increased burden
of disability among preterm babies who survive the neonatal period.
Mortality:
In the last 50 to 60 years the survival rates of premature infants substantially increased because
of technological advances. Preterm births account for approximately 70% of neonatal deaths and
36% of infant deaths, as well as 25-50% of cases of long-term neurologic impairment in
children. The mortality rate is high in developing countries, especially those of Sub-Saharan
Africa. The perinatal mortality rate is 70 deaths per 1000 births; the neonatal mortality rate is 45
deaths per 1000 live births.
In 2023 the Sudan’s neonatal mortality rate (NMR) was estimated as 24.8 per 1,000 live births,
translating to nearly 41,690 new-borns dying annually. The stillbirth rate is estimated to 21.51
deaths per 1,000 births translating into 36,973 annual deaths.
Prematurity challenges:
⮚ Need for advanced respiratory support and care,
⮚ Maintenance of body temperature
⮚ hemodynamic stability,
⮚ Nutrition, feeding.
⮚ maintenance of growth as well as dealing with very delicate and sensitive immature
organs.
Morbidity and complications:
Premature infants are prone to have complications. These complications are gestational age
dependent. Complications are inversely proportionate to gestational age. These complications
can range from devastating intracranial hemorrhage, sepsis, severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia
(chronic lung disease), and necrotizing enterocolitis totalis to minor feeding related issues.
Etiology of prematurity:
Preterm delivery may be:
1. Indicated because of obstetric risks or complications
2. Spontaneous because of preterm labor
indicated preterm delivery Obstetric risks or complications
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends late preterm
delivery in conditions such as multiple gestation with complications, preeclampsia, placenta
previa/ placenta accreta, and prolabor rupture of membranes.
ACOG recommends delivery as early as 32 weeks in selected cases involving multiple gestation
with complications. Quasi-elective delivery earlier than 32 weeks is done on a case-by-case basis
to manage severe maternal and/or fetal complications.
Spontaneous preterm delivery
In an individual patient, spontaneous preterm delivery may or may not have an obvious
immediate trigger (e.g., infection, placental abruption). There are many risk factors:
a-Past obstetric or gynecologic history:
● Prior preterm birth (highest risk)
● Prior cervical conization procedure (cold knife cone or loop electrosurgical excision
procedure)
● Prior dilation and curettage procedure for spontaneous abortion or therapeutic abortion
● Cervical insufficiency, cervical polyps, uterine fibroids, or maternal congenital
reproductive tract abnormalities (e.g., bicornuate uterus)
● Chronic diabetes
● Hypertension
● Kidney disease
b-Obstetric risk factors related to the current pregnancy:
● Short interpregnancy interval (< 6 months)
● Extremes of pre-pregnancy weight (underweight or obese) or of weight gain during
pregnancy (gaining more or less weight than recommended)
● Pregnancy achieved by in vitro fertilization
● Multiple gestation (e.g. twins, triplets)
● Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy
● Placental abruption or placenta previa
● Preterm labor
● Preeclampsia
● Infections (e.g. bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, urinary tract infection, sexually
transmitted infection, intra-amniotic infection)
● Chronic diabetes or gestational diabetes
● Pre-labor rupture of membranes
● Little or no prenatal care
● Certain congenital defects (fetuses with structural congenital heart defects are nearly
twice as likely to be delivered prematurely as fetuses without congenital heart defects)
● Multiple gestation is an important risk factor; 59% of twins and > 98% of higher-order
multiples are delivered prematurely. Many of these infants are very preterm; 10.7% of
twins, 37% of triplets, and > 80% of higher-order multiples are delivered at < 32 weeks
of gestation.
c-Lifestyle or demographic risk factors:
● Younger or older maternal age (eg, < 16 years, > 35 years)
● Non-Hispanic Black or American Indian/Alaska Native women (in the United States)
● Undernutrition
● Cigarette smoking
● Use of alcohol or illicit drugs
● Exposure to certain environmental pollutants
● Domestic violence
● Stress or lack of social support
● Long work hours with long periods of standing
● It is unclear how much risk some of these lifestyle or demographic risk factors contribute
independent of their effect on other risk factors (eg, nutrition, access to medical care).
5.2 Strategies to Prevent Preterm Delivery
1. PROGESTERONE THERAPY
● In women with single gestation pregnancy and a history of spontaneous preterm delivery,
antenatal progesterone therapy is the most effective strategy to decrease the risk of a
recurrent preterm delivery. Progesterone supplementation is beneficial in these women
starting at 16 to 24 weeks’ gestation and continuing through 34 weeks’ gestation.
● women with no history of spontaneous preterm delivery if they have a cervical length of
20 mm or less before 24 weeks’ gestation.
● Progesterone is not beneficial in multiple gestation pregnancies.
2. CERVICAL CERCLAGE AND PESSARY
● Studies have shown that cerclage is associated with a decrease in preterm delivery and in
perinatal death when used in women with a prior preterm delivery and a cervical length
of 25 mm or less.
● The benefit of cerclage in women with a short cervix but no history of a preterm delivery
is uncertain.
● Cerclage is not recommended for multiple gestation pregnancies and has been associated
with a twofold increased risk of preterm delivery (RR = 2.2; 95% CI, 1.2 to 4) in twin
pregnancies.
3.CORTICOSTEROID THERAPY
o Once preterm labor is confirmed, a single course of corticosteroids is the only
intervention for improving neonatal outcomes.
o Betamethasone, two 12-mg doses given intramuscularly 24 hours apart, or
dexamethasone, four 6-mg doses given intramuscularly every 12 hours, is recommended
between 24 and 34 weeks’ gestation, and may be considered as early as 23 weeks’
gestation, in women likely to deliver within seven days regardless of membrane status.
o The use of corticosteroids is associated with decreased neonatal morbidity and mortality.
o Infants whose mothers receive antenatal corticosteroids are less likely to exhibit
respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular hemorrhage, and necrotizing enterocolitis
compared with those whose mothers did not receive corticosteroids.
o Recent data suggest that a second rescue course of antenatal corticosteroids may be
considered if the first dose was given more than seven days earlier and there is still a risk
of preterm delivery before 34 weeks’ gestation.
4.MAGNESIUM SULFATE
• Because of its neuroprotective effect, administration of antenatal magnesium sulfate has
been associated with a decrease in occurrence and severity of cerebral palsy in infants.
5.TOCOLYSIS
• The role of tocolytic /agents is to prolong the time to delivery so that antenatal
corticosteroids and potentially magnesium sulfate can be administered, and the mother
can be transferred to a tertiary care facility with a neonatal intensive care unit.
• Tocolytics have not been shown to directly improve neonatal outcomes, and they are not
always indicated.
• First-line agents used to delay delivery up to 48 hours include calcium channel blockers
(e.g., nifedipine, nicardipine), beta-adrenergic receptor agonists (e.g., terbutaline), and
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as prostaglandin inhibitors (e.g.,
indomethacin, ketorolac).
• Magnesium sulfate can be used as a tocolytic but is associated with significant maternal
adverse effects.

c. Immediate care of the preterm infant:
Preparing appropriately for the delivery and immediate care of the preterm infant is essential when
time permits and may impact on the eventual outcome for the premature infant.
• The level of resuscitation that may be needed is inversely related to the gestation of the
preterm infant.
• Usually, preration taken in resuscitating preterm infants of > 32 completed weeks’
gestation is the same as that taken for term infants. Most need only basic measures such
as drying and stimulation.
• Infants of gestation < 32 weeks (or birth weight< 1500 g) require more active support.
• For infants of < 28weeks’ gestation, this support will probably include endotracheal
intubation and assisted ventilation.
• Ideally, two members of staff who are experienced in the early care of preterm infants
should be present at the delivery of each anticipated infant.
• Before delivery, the attending staff should recheck essential equipment for
resuscitation.

• Although interventions (such as prophylactic antenatal steroids and exogenous surfactants)

palliative care should be provided for the infant and family.

signs of life, such as occasional gasps, after birth.
• Privacy and sensitive support for parents and family with subsequent follow up are
essential.

t: the symptoms of intraventricular hemorrhage
IVH is often asymptomatic but the likelihood of signs increases with the severity of hemorrhage.
The following are the most common symptoms of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH):
• Apnea and bradycardia (stopping breathing and low heart rate)
• Pale or blue coloring (cyanosis)
• Weak suck
• High-pitched cry
• Seizures
• Swelling or bulging of the fontanelles
• Anemia
Diagnosis of intraventricular hemorrhage:
• a complete medical history
• a physical examination,
• Ultrasound Screening
Ultrasound screening
1st Ultrasound
• The first ultrasound should routinely be performed between days 5 and 7 of life.
• This is the optimal time for a single ultrasound examination as all cases of IVH
and >90% of associated parenchymal haemorrhages will be evident .
• However, as many haemorrhages occur on the first day of life and the vast
majority by 48 hours earlier ultrasound examination may be performed on the
basis of clinical concerns or as part of the ongoing research of the unit.
2nd Ultrasound
• The second cranial ultrasound should routinely be performed around day 28 of
life. By this stage parenchymal abnormalities and\or ventriculomegaly will be
evident, providing important prognostic information and guidelines for further
management.
Additional ultrasound scans are indicated in the following circumstances:
• Infants >29 weeks gestation in whom there are clinical concerns or who are
considered to be at significant risk (see risk factors).
• Head circumference growth deviating from the normal intrauterine growth curves.
This situation is most common after Grade III-IV IVH and is indicative of
progressive hydrocephalus.
• Ventriculomegaly on the routine day 28 scan
Prevention of intraventricular Hemorrhage
Antenatal Interventions
• The administration of antenatal corticosteroids to the mother 48 hours prior to
delivery significantly reduces the incidence of IVH and should be considered for
all women at risk of preterm delivery.
• Maternal magnesium sulphate Observational studies have described a reduced
incidence of IVH in the preterm infants of women exposed to intravenous
magnesium sulphate but not all studies support this.
• Management of preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) with
antimicrobial therapy in the expectant management of preterm premature rupture
of the membranes is associated with a significant reduction in the number of
women who deliver within one week and a reduction in chorioamnionitis,
neonatal sepsis and IVH.
Treatment for intraventricular hemorrhage:
There is no specific treatment for IVH.
Sometimes, surgery is necessary to stabilize the condition of the baby.
Apnea of Prematurity
Absence of breathing in the premature infant for a period of > 15 seconds often associated with
bradycardia and/or hypoxia.
Epidemiology
• Recurrent prolonged apnea and bradycardia occurs in most infants under 30 weeks
gestation, in about 50% of infants at 30-32 weeks gestation, and only about 10% of those
at 34-36 weeks gestation.
• The more premature the infant, the greater the possibility of apnea occurring. Apnea of
prematurity is primarily due to immaturity of the respiratory center and control of the
upper airway; most cases are due to a combination of central and obstructive apnea.
• It is important to manage the following additional factors which can either cause or
accentuate apnea:
• Systemic illness - sepsis, hypoxemia, shock.
• CNS – IVH, seizures, asphyxia, cerebral malformations.
• CVS conditions: e.g. PDA
• Anemia
• Drugs - opiates, sedation.
• Post-general anesthesia.
• Metabolic disturbances: hypoglycaemia, hypocalcemia, inborn error of metabolism.
• Hypothermia, hyperthermia.
• Obstructive respiratory problems - macroglossia, micrognathia, tracheomalacia,
• choanal atresia
• Gastro-esophageal reflux.
Management
• Address any underlying factor that may be aggravating apnoeic episodes.
• Monitor infants with cardio-respiratory monitoring and oxygen saturation. Refer to
Monitoring and Observation Frequency.
• If an episode of apnea/bradycardia does not resolve spontaneously, gentle tactile
stimulation maybe required. If response is slow or cyanosis present then bag and mask
ventilation may be needed.
• Prone positioning stabilizes the chest wall, reducing the frequency of apnea.
• CPAP should be optimized. Occasionally non-invasive ventilation (NIPPV) may be
required. Intubation is sometimes required when the above fails.
• Caffeine is a potent cardiac, respiratory and CNS stimulant and is the pharmacological
agent of choice. It has been shown to decrease apnea and reduce the need for ventilator
support. It also reduces short term morbidities such as BPD and ROP, is cost-effective
and improves long term outcomes with lower rates of developmental co-ordination
disorder. For dosage and side effects refer to Neonatal Medication Protocols - Caffeine.
Who to Treat
• Infants < 30 weeks gestation are generally prescribed caffeine routinely. Caffeine has
been shown to reduce post-extubation apnea.
• Infants 30-34 weeks gestation are generally prescribed caffeine if they are symptomatic.
• Consider prescribing caffeine for a neonate in the immediate post-operative period
following a general anesthetic, or prior to immunizations in an ex-preterm neonate.
Stopping Caffeine
• There are no trial data to support decisions to cease treatment.
• Apnea of prematurity decreases with advancing age and can generally be expected to
resolve by 37 weeks corrected gestational age (CGA). Apnea which continues beyond
this period is often multifactorial.
• Caffeine can generally be ceased between 32- & 34-weeks’ gestation, provided the baby
has been stable. Some extremely preterm neonates will require treatment for longer.
• Once the infant has ceased caffeine, infants should remain monitored with an oximeter
for a minimum of 5 days and for 48 hours after the last apnoea/bradycardia. Refer to
Monitoring and Observation Frequency. In general we do not measure caffeine levels
routinely.
• Consider measuring caffeine levels:
• To check therapeutic levels if there are ongoing symptoms.
• If there is concern that caffeine levels may be too high (signs may include persistent
tachycardia).
Respiratory Distress
• The late preterm infant is at high risk for respiratory distress within the first few hours of
birth. Multiple studies have found that late-preterm infants are at
• increased risk for respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), transient tachypnoea of the newborn
(TTN), pneumonia, and air leaks (pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum) requiring
respiratory support with the rate of respiratory
• complications steadily decreasing with each increasing week in gestational age.
• Many late preterm infants are delivered by Caesarean section, which also increases the risk.
• Antepartum steroids have been found to decrease the risk.
• Observe preterm for nasal flaring, tachypnoea, grunting, sternal recessions and cyanosis
Parameters, including respiratory rate, heart rate and temperature should be documented
every 3 hours for the first 12 hours at least, A respiratory rate persistently more than 60/min
is abnormal.
• Oxygen saturations should be measured if the infant has any signs of respiratory distress and
a medical assessment performed.
• Saturations must be measured from the right upper limb (preductal) using an appropriate
oxygen probe and monitor with the probe shielded from ambient light.
• Infants who develop persistent respiratory distress (e.g. tachypnoea, grunting or a persistent
requirement for supplemental oxygen) should be transferred to NICU for further
management
• Respiratory distress can be the result of other conditions such as hypoglycaemia
• Any infant showing respiratory distress should not be allowed to feed orally. If feeds are
ordered they should be via a nasal gastric tube
• To confirm the diagnosis, the medical team may want to take X-rays of the premature baby’s
chest.
• An X-ray of a preemie with RDS will likely show:
Xray finding
• small lung volume
• air bronchograms or air in the airways of the lung that are black in comparison to the
surrounding white areas that do not contain air
• granular-looking areas on the lung where the lung resembles white salt and black pepper
being sprinkled on the film. The more pepper, the more aeration; the more salt, the more
collapse or fluid.
• In suspected cases of RDS, X-rays are not always taken immediately because sometimes
the baby needs to be placed on a ventilator urgently. The chest X-ray is taken after the
baby has been stabilized on the ventilator.

More than 50% of normal newborns and 80% of preterm infants have some jaundice.
Jaundice may be normal or abnormal
Causes of Neonatal Jaundice
Physiological Jaundice : Appears after 24 hours, peaks at day 3–5, resolves by 1–2 weeks.
Pathological Jaundice : Jaundice that appears within 24 hours, is excessively high, rises rapidly,
lasting > 14 days in term and > 21 days in preterm infant, mainly due to Increased Bilirubin
Production (Haemolysis)
o Haemolytic disease of the newborn (blood group incompatibility)

o Red cell membrane defects
o Sepsis with haemolysis
other causes

• congenital syphilis or other intrauterine infection

Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)
Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is an irreversible but preventable leading cause of childhood
and lifelong visual disability.
Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), first known as "retrolental fibroplasia," is a major blinding
disease among children in the United States (US). Thus far, 3 "epidemics" of ROP-induced
blindness have been reported. The first epidemic was seen in the 1940s and 1950s in developed
countries, most commonly associated with unregulated supplementary oxygen. After regulating
and monitoring at birth of high oxygen (ROP virtually disappeared) the survival rates of preterm
infants at ever-earlier gestational age, to eventually also lower birth weights with re-emergence
of ROP as a major problem is chronicled in the second epidemic that started in industrialised
countries from 1970s. Finally in the mid-1990s, the third epidemic began in low- and middle-
income nations (first in Eastern Europe and Latin America, expanding to East and South Asia
and finally to sub-Saharan Africa) due to both high rates of preterm delivery and varied levels of
new-born care in these countries. Some countries or regions within countries lack the equipment
and resources to optimise their care, and typically ROP is detected in larger and older new-borns
exposed to unregulated oxygen (similar to what had occurred in the US decades earlier).
Etiology:
In utero, the fetus is in a hypoxic state. When infants are born prematurely, the relative oxygen
level is sometimes increased even when oxygenation is at ambient levels. High supplemental
oxygen can be damaging to capillaries.
The cause of ROP is premature birth and additional factors that cause a mismatch between
normal retinal vascularization and the oxygen need of the developing retina. There is also
consideration of maternal factors affecting nutrition and inflammation/infection.
ROP is a dynamic pathology, does not presented at birth, but after 2-3 weeks, for this the parents
should be worn about the risk of developing ROP in their preterm baby. So, the early retinal
examination should be in NICU or immediately after discharge, then repeat the fundus
examination after 3-4 weeks searching for signs of progression or regression of the condition,
ROP visual loss control strategies:
It requires efficient collaboration within different specialties (Obstetrician, midwife,
Neonatologist, ophthalmologist).
Primary Measures:
• follow up of preterm deliveries.
• antenatal steroid for threatened preterm deliveries.
• in-suite transfer for an equipped facility with NICU for threatened preterm deliveries.
• delayed umbilical cord clamping (ideally after 60 to 90 seconds),
• promoting kangaroo care.
• Early provision of breast milk,
• gentle resuscitation-use CPAP.
• avoid 100% unmonitored O2 supplement-use oximeters, and use oximeters and set
saturation target and alarm).
• prevent sepsis (good hygiene, aseptic techniques)
• promote breast feeding.
• avoid blood transfusion (consult neonatologist).
Secondary Measures:
• 1st or 2nd indirect ophthalmoscopy at 4 weeks postnatal age.
• Repeat in 1 or 2 weeks depending on retinal vascularization.
• early detection, classification, and timely management of sight threatening-ROP.
• If Type 1 ROP or plus disease suspected, refer to tertiary centers.
Tertiary measures:
• confirm the diagnosis.
• treatment protocole (laser photocoagulation, Intravitreal anti-VEGF, of complex retinal
surgery)
• follow-up regularlly until regreeion or advancement of the condition.

Section (6) Kangaroo Mother Care
KMC definition
Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is an evidence-based method of care for premature and low-
birth-weight infants (specifically those birth weight less than 2 kg ) that involves skin-to-skin
contact with the mother (or father or caregiver) and exclusive and frequent breastfeeding.
Importance and benefits:
KMC regulates baby’s temperature, heart rate, breathing and oxygen saturation, reduces
incidence of apnoea and bradycardia and associated with better neurodevelopment
6.1 KMC indication and Contraindication
indications:
Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is indicated for neonates who are preterm and/or have low birth
weight, specifically those with birth weight less than 2,000 grams.
contraindications:
• Major congenital malformation
• Ongoing seizure activity
• Sever jaundice requiring immediate management (e.g. exchange transfusion)
• Life threatening instability
• Inability of parent or caregiver to provide KMC (including medical or psychological or
social reason or refusal to consent
6.2 KMC place and equipment
Place for KMC:
The area chosen for KMC should be quite, warm (22-24°C) and insure privacy. It can be NICU
. SCNU, postnatal ward, breastfeeding rooms, at bed side or at home after proper training
Equipment and supply:
Available and affordable equipment and supplies which can make the mothers stay more
comfortable during KMC can be used
Beds: Comfortable beds and/or chairs for the mothers, if possible adjustable or with enough
pillows to maintain an upright or semi-recumbent position for resting and sleeping.
Curtains: can help to ensure privacy in a room with several beds.
Other equipment and supplies like a thermometer, scales, basic resuscitation equipment, and
oxygen where possible, should be available where preterm babies are cared for; drugs for
preventing and treating frequent problems of preterm newborn babies may be added according to
local protocols.
6.3 KMC Parent and infant preparation
Discuss benefits of kangaroo care for both parents and baby at any available opportunity
Daily shower or washing is sufficient for maternal/ parental hygiene;
Strict hand-washing should be encouraged after using the toilet and changing the baby.
Mother Clothing: the mother can wear whatever she finds comfortable and warm, provided the
dress accommodates the baby,
Health facility should provide clean sheets or aprons for mothers and babies.
Clothing for the baby:
When the ambient temperature is 22-24°C, the baby is carried in kangaroo position naked,
except for the diaper, a warm hat and socks .
When the temperature drops below 22°C, baby should wear a cotton, sleeveless shirt, open at the
front to allow the face, chest, abdomen, arms and legs to remain in skin-to-skin contact with the
mother’s chest and abdomen. The mother then covers herself and the baby with her usual dress.

Section (7) Neonatal Procedures
Introduction:
This chapter encompasses a range of interventions and procedures that are important for
emergency and ongoing care of neonate at. Mastery of these skills by healthcare professionals is
essential to provide timely, effective, and safe care to neonates, ultimately improving neonatal
outcomes and reducing the burden of neonatal morbidity and mortality.
This chapter aims to
● Standardize neonatal care practices
● Enhance the competency of healthcare personnel
● Ultimately improve neonatal outcomes.
